description: The atmosphere is the protective envelope of gases surrounding the Earth. Variations in temperature and atmospheric pressure across different latitudes lead to the formation of both global planetary and local wind systems.

sections.title: Composition of the Atmosphere
sections.description: The atmosphere is a complex mechanical mixture of various gases, water vapor, and dust particles.

important_facts.fact: Nitrogen (78.08%) is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere, followed by Oxygen (20.95%).
Argon (0.93%) is the third most abundant gas and is categorized as an inert or noble gas.
Carbon Dioxide (0.036%) is a crucial greenhouse gas responsible for the greenhouse effect and maintaining Earth's ambient temperature.

sections.title: Structure of the Atmosphere
sections.description: Based on temperature variations with altitude, the atmosphere is divided into five distinct layers.

key_concepts.explanation: The lowest and most important layer. All weather phenomena, such as cloud formation, rainfall, and storms, occur exclusively in this layer.

Located above the troposphere, it is free from clouds and weather disturbances, making it ideal for flying aeroplanes. It contains the crucial Ozone Layer which absorbs harmful Ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun.
The coldest layer of the atmosphere. Most meteorites entering the Earth's atmosphere from space burn up in this layer due to friction.
Contains electrically charged particles called ions. This layer reflects radio waves back to Earth, making long-distance radio communication possible.
The outermost layer of the atmosphere that gradually merges into outer space. It is extremely rarefied and contains light gases like Helium and Hydrogen.

sections.title: Pressure Belts and Coriolis Force
sections.description: The Earth's rotation and unequal heating by the sun create distinct pressure belts and deflective forces.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: An apparent force generated by the Earth's rotation on its axis that deflects moving objects, including winds.
scientific_principles.application: According to Ferrel's Law, the Coriolis force deflects winds to their right in the Northern Hemisphere and to their left in the Southern Hemisphere.

key_concepts.explanation: The zone located between 5° North and 5° South of the equator. It is characterized by extremely calm atmospheric conditions and weak, variable winds.
High-pressure zones located between 30° and 35° latitudes in both hemispheres. Historically, ships were becalmed here, and sailors threw horses overboard to conserve water and lighten the load.

sections.title: Planetary or Permanent Winds
sections.description: Winds that blow constantly throughout the year in a particular direction from high-pressure to low-pressure belts.

key_concepts.explanation: These winds blow steadily from the Sub-tropical High to the Equatorial Low pressure belts. They were highly utilized by early merchants and sailors for oceanic trade routes.

Winds blowing from the Sub-tropical High to the Sub-polar Low pressure belts (60°-65°). They are exceptionally strong and consistent in the Southern Hemisphere due to vast, unbroken oceanic expanses (e.g., known as Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties).
Extremely cold and dry winds that blow from the Polar High pressure belts (90°) towards the Sub-polar Low pressure belts.

sections.title: Major Local Winds of the World
sections.description: Winds driven by local temperature and pressure differences that influence the climate of specific geographical regions.

key_associations.extra_info: A warm and dry wind. It is famously called the 'Snow Eater' because it rapidly melts snow and clears pastures for livestock grazing in winter.
A warm, dry wind primarily affecting Switzerland. It raises the temperature and significantly aids in the rapid ripening of grapes.
A hot, dust-laden wind blowing from the Sahara. When it crosses the Mediterranean and reaches Italy, it causes rain mixed with red sand, famously termed 'Blood Rain'.
An extremely cold and dry wind that blows violently down the Rhone River Valley towards the Mediterranean Sea, often damaging crops.
An intensely hot and dry summer wind that blows in the afternoons during May and June, occasionally causing fatal heatstrokes.
